newsitem.title: INDIA: India mulls credit rating rules after firm crashes.
newsitem.headline: India mulls credit rating rules after firm crashes.

text.p: Indian regulators, shocked by the failure of a firm that swallowed thousands of investors' savings, are drawing up rules to tighten the practices of credit rating agencies that have a strong influence on investors' decisions.

The action follows the collapse last month of the CRB group, accused of irregularities in financial services. Angry investors have lashed out at a credit rating agency that they say awarded high ratings to the fixed deposit scheme of a CRB group firm despite the irregularities.

V. Ranjan, executive director of market regulator the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), said on Thursday SEBI was in talks with India's major credit rating agencies, but gave no timeframe for the new rules.
Indian federal police investigating CRB's collapse estimate its liabilities at 9.32 billion rupees ($260 million).
CRB chairman Chain Roop Bhansali has said he wants to return the investors' money. He was detained by police on Monday until the expected completion of the investigation in two weeks' time.
Investors who fear they may lose everything say the regulatory authorities failed in their duties.
Investor anger has also been directed at rating agency Credit Analysis and Research (CARE), which gave CRB's scheme a top A+ rating in February 1994 and downgraded it to A in September last year.
It was only after the central bank banned CRB from accepting further deposits in April that CARE slashed the rating to C, and then dropped it to its lowest rating D in May.

"The rating agency continued to place the company's fixed deposit programme as an upper medium grade investment with adequate principal and interest safety till April 1997," the Centre for Monitoring the Indian Economy, an independent think-tank, said in its May review of the economy.
Officials at CARE were unavailable to comment.
Concern over operations of other Indian rating agencies has followed in the wake of the CRB collapse.
"The role of the credit rating agencies has come as a great shock in many ways," said economist Kirit Parikh, director of the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research.
"But this is a new area, there will always be a market shake-up. Some credit rating agencies are good, and some bad."

A banking analyst with the Indian affiliate of a foreign investment bank said he doubted if regulations for credit rating agencies would work. Businessmen tended to shop around for favourable ratings, he said.
"Credit rating agencies are difficult to regulate, because (ratings are) so personal and subjective," the analyst said.

"Because there are three or four of them (ratings agencies), people have been playing around with them -- but leave it to market forces and it'll sort itself out, though in the interim period there'll be some problems."
The chief of a credit rating agency said agencies were hampered in their work not only by gaps in the information firms gave them but by rapid changes in the business.

"There are serious fundamental changes which reflect the volatility in the environment," he told Reuters. "So the rating is volatile and will be volatile. To expect the ratings to remain stable is irrational."
Despite appearances, he said the rating agencies had done a good job. "I don't think the agencies should be held reponsible for deviations from the plans submitted to them," he added.

R. Shankar Raman, senior vice-president of L&T Finance Ltd. said there were too few rating agencies to cope with India's non-bank financial companies, of which there are estimated to be 45,000, with half of them active.
